Above Reproach (Blameless)
uh-BUV rih-PROHCH
adjective (church polity)
From Greek anepilemptos (1 Tim 3:2), "not able to be laid hold of," and anenkletos (Titus 1:6), "not arraigned"; rendered blameless, from Old English blame through Latin blasphemare.

Biblical Definition

Above reproach is the overarching qualification under which every other mark of the elder gathers. Paul opens the list with it: "A bishop then must be blameless" (1 Tim 3:2), and to Titus, "If any be blameless" (Titus 1:6), repeating it as he names the office, "For a bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God" (Titus 1:7). The Greek anepilemptos pictures a man who offers no handle, no projecting hook by which an accuser may seize and drag him; anenkletos pictures a man against whom no charge can be made to stick in court. The word does not mean sinless — no man this side of glory is that — but it means without scandal, without a settled and visible blot that would shame the gospel and silence his rebuke of others. The deacon too must be "found blameless" after proving (1 Tim 3:10). Such a life is the soil in which all the particular virtues grow: hospitality, sobriety, gentleness, and aptness to teach are the shape that blamelessness takes. This dictionary confesses that Christ requires of His overseers a life that gives the watching world and the accusing devil no purchase, that the name of God be not blasphemed through His ministers.

Webster 1828 Definition

The chief and summary qualification of an elder: a life so ordered that no accusation can take hold. It renders the Greek anepilemptos and anenkletos, meaning not sinless but without settled scandal, and it governs all the particular virtues that follow.

ABOVE REPROACH, adjective. Blameless; offering no handle by which an accuser may lay hold.

It translates the apostle's anepilemptos and anenkletos, the heading qualification of the bishop and the deacon.

"A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober" (1 Tim 3:2).

It requires not perfection but the absence of any open and disqualifying blot upon the man's name and walk.

It is the root from which hospitality, sobriety, and aptness to teach grow as its branches.

Key Scripture

1 Tim 3:2 — "A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach;"

Titus 1:6 — "If any be blameless, the husband of one wife, having faithful children not accused of riot or unruly."

Titus 1:7 — "For a bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God; not selfwilled, not soon angry, not given to wine, no striker, not given to filthy lucre;"

1 Tim 3:10 — "And let these also first be proved; then let them use the office of a deacon, being found blameless."

Modern Corruption

Blamelessness is hollowed out where reputation is managed rather than character formed, and where a settled scandal is excused as a private matter that need not touch a man's public office.

expand to see more

The age prizes image over integrity, the curated reputation over the proven walk. But anepilemptos asks whether there is in fact a hook to be grasped, not merely whether the man has hidden it well. A church satisfied with the appearance of blamelessness, while tolerating known and unrepented sin in its officers, has not kept the qualification but counterfeited it. The remedy is the apostolic order: "let these also first be proved" (1 Tim 3:10) — tested in the open over time, not waved through on charm.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The positive principle to recover is that blamelessness is the indispensable platform for rebuke. An elder must "by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers" (Titus 1:9); a man with an open blot cannot wield the sword, for his own life answers him. The church should therefore prize quiet, long-tested faithfulness in her candidates above brilliance, knowing that a blameless walk lends weight to every word.

Hebrew Roots

The term gathers two Greek words, anepilemptos and anenkletos, both prefixed with the negative a-, denying any grip or charge against the man.

expand to see more

Greek anepilemptos (1 Tim 3:2): not epilambano, not able to be laid hold of.

Greek anenkletos (Titus 1:6): not enkaleo, not called into court or arraigned.

The negative prefix a- in both denies, not the existence of sin, but the existence of a disqualifying handle.

English blameless traces through Latin blasphemare, the very evil a scandalous officer invites (1 Tim 6:1).

The legal flavour of anenkletos recalls the courtroom: no charge can be made to stand.

Usage

"The candidate was gifted, but he was not above reproach, and the elders rightly delayed his ordination."

"To be above reproach is not to be sinless but to give the accuser no handle to seize."

"An officer above reproach can rebuke the gainsayer, for his own walk does not answer him back."
